transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-03-15 14:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Liam Carter, Priya Nair (Redwood); Mark Reynolds, Tara Singh, Jamal Ortiz, Aisha Khan (Crescentpay)

Summary (auto): weekly POC check-in focused on latency tuning (TTFT, streaming, seq len, kernels). Action items captured below.

[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Mark Reynolds: Mark here.
[00:08] Tara Singh: Tara on from MLOps.
[00:10] Jamal Ortiz: Jamal, SRE.
[00:12] Aisha Khan: Aisha, product.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, SE.
[00:17] Liam Carter: Cool. Agenda — quick pass on last week items, TTFT numbers from staging, streaming anomalies, kernel choices and sequence length effects, and then next steps.

[02:05] Priya Nair: Ok so first point — TTFT. We re-ran the bench with the updated micro-batching config. Baseline TTFT for 2k seq (non-streaming) was 220ms median, p95 ~380ms on H100 reserved nodes. However, you reported higher in your staging traces — Tara, can you remind us what you saw?
[02:28] Tara Singh: Yeah, in staging p50 was like 300ms and p95 got to 600ms sometimes. There's a weird bump at around 30 requests per second where it feels like there's a kernel fallback? Could be quantization mismatch or different compiled kernel selection. Also our traffic is a mix — half of sessions are short customer support queries ~100 tokens and the other half are multi-turn summaries ~1.2k tokens.

[04:02] Priya Nair: That mix explains a lot. When sequence lengths vary widely, the runtime sometimes chooses different attention kernels mid-run; that causes small jitters in TTFT because of on-the-fly kernel paths. We recommended pinning the short-request path to the fast streaming kernel and enabling prefix/KV cache for multi-turns.

[05:10] Jamal Ortiz: Quick question — you're saying kernel is chosen dynamically? That seems risky for consistent latency.
[05:18] Priya Nair: It is dynamic: compilation + kernel selector picks best kernel for current shape. For highest predictability we can force a kernel profile or use our 'low-variance' runtime mode which biases toward stable kernels and slightly higher average throughput. There's a tradeoff.

[06:00] Mark Reynolds: What's the TTFT impact if we go low-variance? We care about p95 for customer interactions.
[06:07] Priya Nair: In our tests low-variance mode increased median by ~10-20ms but reduced p95 by ~80-120ms on H100 for mixed workloads. So p95 improves.

[07:05] Liam Carter: We also saw that streaming vs non-streaming had different effective TTFT. For small messages streaming gives earlier first token because of chunked decoding, but for many interleaved streaming requests kernels sometimes suffer because of fragmentation.

[07:40] Tara Singh: We definitely want streaming for live chat. But the summary pipeline could be batched non-streaming. Can you recommend config for both?

[08:00] Priya Nair: Yes: for chat short messages — enable streaming, keep batch size small (2-4), and set idle flush to 30ms. For summary workloads use non-streaming with larger batch windows and enable continuous KV cache when multi-turn. We'll send concrete config examples.

[09:30] Aisha Khan: Is there a cost hit for low-variance kernel or forcing a kernel? Finance will ask.
[09:36] Priya Nair: Slight — you might lose some throughput efficiency so cost per token could go up ~3-6% depending on load shape. But if p95 SLAs are critical it's usually worth it; we can model costs in the benchmark sheet.

[11:00] Liam Carter: Tara, you mentioned a kernel fallback around 30 RPS. Do you have a trace we can look at?
[11:08] Tara Singh: Yes uploaded a couple logs to the shared drive (link: drive.redwood.internal/crescentpay/ttft-traces). One trace shows spikes exactly when a long request joins a short-stream heavy window.

[12:20] Priya Nair: Ok will pull that. My suspicion is the runtime decides to switch to a different attention kernel to handle long sequences and that causes one-off compilation or path changes. There shouldn't be compile-on-demand in production but fallback selection can happen when shapes change.

[13:45] Jamal Ortiz: Can we force the model variant to a shorter-seq optimized checkpoint for chat and route summaries to a long-seq variant?
[13:53] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Smart routing by model variant is something we recommend — route streaming chat to a trimmed context model or a lower-precision quantized variant optimized for TTFT. Summaries go to long-context variant. The platform supports automatic routing rules.

[15:10] Mark Reynolds: About quantization — we tried 4-bit and saw slight hallucination increase for summaries. Any tips?
[15:20] Priya Nair: For generative quality, prefer q8_0 for summaries if quality matters. q4 may be fine for short chat where you prioritize latency/cost, but you'll need regression tests. We can run evals tied to your prompt sets.

[16:00] Liam Carter: On the hardware side — you're on H100 in staging, right?
[16:04] Tara Singh: Yes H100 reserved nodes on your dedicated pool.

[16:20] Priya Nair: Good. Kernel differences between A100 and H100 manifest differently for long sequences; H100 gives better throughput for long seq but compiling optimized kernels for H100 can yield different TTFT behavior. We'll include A100 vs H100 notes in the recommendations.

[18:00] Aisha Khan: What's the timeline for the next set of benchmarks?
[18:04] Liam Carter: We'll run targeted bench with your exact seq distribution and the mixed traffic shape by Friday. We'll push the sheet by Mon.

[18:30] Priya Nair: Also, KV cache behavior: ensure your session affinity keeps requests hitting the same backend so prefix cache is effective. If you're load-balancing incorrectly you'll see cache misses causing token regen and latency spikes. Jamal any constraints on affinity?
[18:50] Jamal Ortiz: We currently use round-robin LB across pods; adding sticky session looks doable with the LB cookie. We'll try that in staging.

[21:00] Mark Reynolds: Can you explain streaming buffer sizing? We've seen buffer stalls causing hesitations mid-response.

[21:12] Priya Nair: Buffering is controlled by chunk size and flush threshold. If chunk too small you get more frequent network chatter; if too big you delay first token. For chat use chunk ~64-128 tokens, flush threshold 20-30ms. For low-latency, prefer smaller chunks and aggressive flushing but that increases CPU overhead.

[23:00] Tara Singh: We've got two environments — staging and preprod. Staging currently simulates 200 concurrent chat sessions; preprod has synthetic higher seq summaries. Which should we prioritize?

[23:12] Liam Carter: Prioritize staging chat for p95 SLA and preprod for throughput optimization. We'll run two bench passes.

[25:00] Priya Nair: One more note — there was a small mismatch in the model configs: your agent was using an older KV cache TTL. That caused some cache invalidation churn, increasing avg latency. Update TTL to session length + 10% and that should reduce cache misses.

[27:00] Jamal Ortiz: Noted. We'll bump TTL and re-run.

[28:30] Mark Reynolds: Any surprises in memory usage? Some team members saw OOM-ish errors on one node during bulk summaries.

[28:40] Priya Nair: That was likely due to peak concurrent long-seq batching hitting the memory cliff. We recommend capping max batch size for long sequences and using workspace reservation settings. We'll include exact configs.

[30:00] Aisha Khan: For the pilot, what qualifies as success next week?

[30:08] Liam Carter: Hit p95 <= 450ms for chat on 95% of traffic shapes and no OOMs for summary jobs under the expected throughput. Also have the cost model validated.

[31:20] Tara Singh: Ok sounds good. We'll run two sample runs and upload traces.

[33:00] Priya Nair: Quick demo note — there's a flag in the console to force 'low-variance kernel' per model route. I'll show that in the follow-up demo if you want.

[34:12] Mark Reynolds: Yes please include that. Also include the exact CLI commands for kernel pinning.

[35:00] Liam Carter: We'll capture CLI + console steps in the doc pack.

[36:40] Jamal Ortiz: On observability — curious if Redwood can surface per-token timing broken into scheduling/compute/serialize?

[36:48] Priya Nair: Yes the console has token-level breakdown, and we can enable trace hooks to export to your Datadog/Prometheus. That will help pinpoint TTFT stalls.

[38:10] Aisha Khan: Any risk with security or autonomy in changing kernel modes?

[38:20] Priya Nair: No security risk — it's runtime behavior. For Private deployments you control policy; for Hosted we'll apply via your route settings. Audit logs show changes.

[40:00] Liam Carter: Alright let's recap action items.

[40:05] Liam Carter: Redwood: share updated benchmark sheet and kernel recommendations; provide config snippets for streaming and non-streaming; include A100 vs H100 notes.

[40:18] Priya Nair: And provide CLI steps for low-variance and kernel pinning.

[40:24] Tara Singh: CrescentPay: share sequence length histograms, re-run traces with sticky sessions, and run streaming vs non-streaming comparison.

[41:30] Mark Reynolds: We'll aim to get traces by Tuesday and confirm next sync.

[42:00] Liam Carter: Next sync — same time next week? 14:00 PDT next Thursday?

[42:08] Tara Singh: Works for us.

[42:12] Aisha Khan: Fine.

[44:00] Liam Carter: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the sheet and the example configs.

[44:06] Priya Nair: Thanks all.

[44:30] (meeting ends)
